note: The story steps back a little: Canto 7 ended with the poets already at the foot of the tower. Boccaccio tells a tale that Dante wrote the first seven cantos in Florence, lost them when he was exiled, and took the poem up again here. Most scholars doubt it.
A watchtower on the near shore of the marsh, reached at the end of Canto 7. Hell's lower city is guarded like a fortress of Dante's own time.

A signal, as castles of the time signaled with fires by night. The two flames are usually read as announcing two newcomers. A tower far across the water, on the walls of the city ahead, answers with one.

context: The poets stand on its shore. The wrathful fight each other in its mud, and the sullen lie sunk beneath the surface (Canto 7).

note: Phlegyas speaks to one soul only. He seems to take Dante for a new arrival sent down to the marsh, and does not yet see that he is alive.

context: A man destroyed by his own rage ferries souls across the marsh of the wrathful. As with Charon and Minos, Virgil silences him with a word.

quote: Only when I entered did it seem to bear weight
note: Virgil is a shade and weighs nothing. Dante's living body makes the boat ride low. In the Aeneid, Charon's boat groans and takes in water under the living Aeneas.
Before death. The soul sees that Dante is alive.
Dante has recognized a fellow Florentine. The other souls shout his name a few lines on.

The Italian is alma sdegnosa, a scornful or indignant soul. Virgil praises Dante's anger as the right kind: indignation against evil, the opposite of the blind rage punished here. It is the first time in Hell that Dante shows a sinner no pity.

quote: blessed is the woman who carried you
note: An echo of Luke 11:27, where a woman in the crowd calls out to Christ: "Blessed is the womb that bore you." It is the only mention of Dante's mother in the poem.
The powerful who trust in their rank. Pride and rage go together in this scene: the man in the mud was arrogant in life, and is furious in death.

quote: praise and thank God for what I saw
note: Dante's pleasure in this has troubled many readers. The poem's answer is that to hate sin is to side with God's justice. But the feeling is plainly personal too: this was a neighbor and an enemy.

context: The muddy soul who rose beside the boat, named only now, by the others who fall on him.

note: Rage with no one left to strike turns on itself. The wrathful of this marsh tear each other with their teeth (Canto 7), and Argenti bites his own flesh.

context: Its walls come into view across the marsh. Everything so far has been upper Hell.

note: The Italian gravi means heavy: weighed down by graver sins and heavier pains than those above. The "great host" is the army of devils that garrisons the city.
Dante's word is meschite, mosques. To a Christian of 1300, a skyline of mosques meant a city of a rival faith: this is the capital of God's enemy.

Hell has two parts. The circles above the wall punish sins of weakness: lust, gluttony, greed, anger. Inside the city are the sins of malice, chosen with the will. Virgil explains the plan in Canto 11.
In the Aeneid, Tartarus, the prison of the worst sinners, is a walled fortress with a tower of iron, ringed by a river of fire. Aeneas only looks at it from outside. Dante will go in.
The rebel angels, thrown out of Heaven with Lucifer and now devils. They are the first devils Dante meets, and the first guardians who refuse to give way.
The devils use the word Dante used of himself in Inferno 2, when he feared the journey would be madness. They speak to his deepest fear: being left to find the way back alone.
The first time Dante turns and speaks to the reader directly. He does it about twenty times in the poem, usually at a moment of fear or wonder.
A round number in the Bible's manner, meaning many times. Virgil has saved him from the she-wolf and from Charon, Minos, Cerberus, Plutus, Phlegyas and Argenti, among others.
God, whose name Virgil avoids in Hell. The journey was willed in Heaven, as he told Charon and Minos.

quote: yes and no battling in my head
note: Will Virgil come back, or not? Will they get through, or not?
Virgil's first failure. Until now his word alone has cleared the way. Read as allegory, human reason can deal with the sins of weakness, but against hardened malice it needs help from Heaven.
The city of Dis.

The outer gate of Hell, in Canto 3. Tradition held that the devils tried to bar it against Christ when he came down to free the righteous dead (see Inferno 4). He broke it open, and it has stood without locks ever since.
The words over Hell's gate in Canto 3, which end by telling all who enter to abandon hope. Dante's Italian calls it the dead writing: the writing of death.

quote: one who will open this city to us
note: A messenger from Heaven is already on the way down. Virgil knows help was promised, and the next canto shows it arrive.
